summary: This informational RFC documents a DHCPv4 option previously defined privately by Cisco for subnet allocation. It lets a client request a dynamically allocated subnet, learn what was allocated, and report usage statistics, and documents it in line with RFC 3942.

eli5.summary: Normally you ask for one house number. This lets a router ask for a whole street of numbers and report how many it used.

subtitle: Cisco's privately defined DHCPv4 option, now documented, that lets a client lease a whole subnet instead of one address.

tldr.problem: Cisco had a DHCPv4 option, number 220, in use for allocating whole subnets, and RFC 3942 asked vendors to document such pre-existing uses of option numbers in the range 128-223.
tldr.mechanism: One option carries suboptions to request a subnet, describe the subnet offered, name it and suggest a lease time. Clients lease, renew and release subnets with the normal DHCP messages and can report usage statistics.
tldr.outcome: Published for information only. The DHC working group had no input into the protocol, makes no statement about its correctness, and saw no interest in further implementation or deployment other than privately.

today: RFC 6656 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It documents an existing private option for the record and does not make it a standard.

sections.title: Why This Option Is Documented
sections.content:
This memo documents the Subnet Allocation option, which Cisco developed so that a DHCP client could allocate a subnet using information from a DHCP server. It uses DHCP option number 220, one of the numbers reclassified by RFC 3942. That RFC gave vendors six months to tell the DHC working group and IANA that they used such numbers and would document the usage in an RFC. This memo is that documentation.

The RFC is frank about its standing. The DHC working group had no input into the details, makes no statement about correctness, and saw no interest in further implementation or deployment other than privately, so it is published solely for information.

The option is described as a straightforward way to allocate a subnet from DHCP. It suits a simple dial-in aggregation box, or a hierarchical chain of DHCP servers, each leasing subnets to the next one down.
sections.eli5: A company built its own way to hand out whole blocks of addresses. The rule-makers asked it to write the details down, so this is the write-up.

sections.title: The Option and Its Suboptions
sections.content:
The option starts with a code (220), a length and a flags byte (no flags are currently defined), followed by suboptions. One option number serves every function; the suboption numbers select the function.

  • Subnet-Request (suboption 1): sent by the client. It is always 2 bytes long and holds a flags byte and a requested prefix length. The h flag says whether the client will allocate addresses from the subnet itself (1) or relay requests to the server (0). The i flag says the client only wants information about subnets already allocated to it. A prefix of 0 means no length is suggested.
  • Subnet-Information (suboption 2): carries one or more Subnet Prefix Information blocks. The c flag marks information about previously allocated subnets, and the s flag says the server has more to tell the client.
  • Subnet-Name (suboption 3): a UTF-8 name such as a department or address pool, passed to the server for use during allocation.
  • Suggested-Lease-Time (suboption 4): a 4-octet lease time the server may include. The client should use the lesser of this and the remaining lease time of the subnet itself.

Each prefix information block holds a 4-octet network number, a prefix length, a flags byte with a deprecate flag (d) and the h flag, and a statistics length that is zero when no statistics are included.
sections.eli5: The option is a form with several boxes. One box says how big a block you want, one describes the block you got, one gives it a label, and one suggests how long you can keep it.

sections.title: Requesting and Renewing a Subnet
sections.content:
Allocation follows the usual DHCP exchange. The client sends a DHCPDISCOVER with a Subnet-Request. The prefix length must be 0 or from 1 to 30. The server answers with a DHCPOFFER holding Subnet-Information suboptions, and must not echo the Subnet-Request. The client then sends a DHCPREQUEST containing only Subnet-Information, unmodified, though it may leave out some offered subnets. The server answers with a DHCPACK and may remove subnets from the list, but must not change network numbers or prefix lengths.

A packet exchange cannot provide subnet allocation and address assignment at once: the server should set yiaddr to 0.0.0.0 and the client must ignore address assignment fields. One IP address lease time option covers every subnet in a message, and each subnet, identified by its network number and prefix length, can be renewed or released individually.

The client must renew subnet leases much as it renews an address. A server may reply with a DHCPACK or a DHCPNAK. On a DHCPNAK the client must immediately stop using the subnet. A DHCPACK with the deprecate flag set tells the client to stop handing out addresses from the subnet and send a DHCPRELEASE once every address has been returned. A server may also send a DHCPFORCERENEW (RFC 3203) to make the client renew one subnet.
sections.eli5: You ask for a block, the server shows you one, you say yes, and it is yours for a while. Before time runs out you ask to keep it, and when you are done you hand it back.

sections.title: Usage Statistics and Recovering State
sections.content:
In renew and release messages a client may report how it is using a subnet. The statistics come in a fixed order: High water (the most addresses ever allocated at one time), Currently in use, and Unusable (for example after a DHCPDECLINE). A value of 0xffff skips a field, and new statistics may only be appended after the existing ones. Servers should always send a statistics length of zero.

A client that has restarted and lost its records can ask the server what it holds. It sends a DHCPDISCOVER with the i flag set and a prefix of 0. The server returns the first of its ordered list of subnets for that client with the c flag set, and sets the s flag if there are more. The client sends the last Subnet-Information back to the same server to get the next set, until s is 0.

How the server actually picks subnets, and which networks may be subnetted, is left to the implementation.
sections.eli5: The router can tell the server how many addresses it handed out. If the router forgets everything after a reboot, it can ask the server to list its blocks again, a few at a time.

sections.title: Comparison with DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation
sections.content: The RFC lists how this option differs from DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (RFC 3633). There is nothing like an IA_PD. A server that cannot allocate a subnet stays silent instead of sending a refusal. DHCPv6 has no way to return usage statistics, no deprecation flag, no subnet name suboption and no suggested lease time. Prefix Delegation also corresponds only to the hierarchical case, where the h flag is set; there is no version in which the server keeps authority over the addresses.
sections.eli5: The newer IPv6 way of handing out address blocks is simpler. It cannot report usage, cannot say a block is going away soon, and always gives the router full control.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security section points to the exposures discussed in RFC 2131 and warns that the Subnet Allocation option can be used to hoard all allocable subnets on a network. Implementations should consider the DHCP Authentication option (RFC 3118) if more security is needed.

IANA assigned DHCP option number 220 in accordance with RFC 3942. No suboption values were assigned; new ones may only be defined by IETF Consensus, meaning RFCs approved by the IESG.
sections.eli5: A greedy client could grab every block of addresses on the network. Servers that worry about this can make clients prove who they are.
